title: Age, Sex, and Finish Time as Determinants of Pacing in the Marathon
authors: March DS, Vanderburgh PM, Titlebaum PJ, Hoops ML
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 186 men and 133 women finishers of three editions (2005-2007) of a midwestern U.S. marathon on a 1.6 km loop course; ambient temperature never above 5 C
findings: Pacing was defined as the mean velocity of the last 9.7 km divided by that of the first 32.5 km (closer to 1.0 is better pacing).
Age, sex and run time each were significant independent determinants of pacing in a multiple regression.
The authors conclude that older, women and faster runners were better pacers than younger, men and slower marathoners, respectively.
Ambient temperature never exceeded 5 C, so hyperthermia was not expected to affect pacing.
limitations: Cool conditions only; one loop course with pace markers; 319 finishers from one race; the regression coefficients are not legible in the abstract (symbols lost in the indexed text), so only the direction is recorded; association, not a trial of any pacing instruction.
implications: Descriptive support that slower finishers hold pace less well over the last quarter of a marathon than faster finishers, in the cool. It is not a target shape and gives no per-kilometre pace.

verification.notes: Crossref matches title, journal, year, authors (JSCR 25:386-391). Abstract read on Europe PMC and PubMed; the regression statistics are garbled in the indexed abstract, so no coefficient is quoted. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
